chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ayoub ibn Nuh, raising it (narrating) from Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) who said:

When a piece is cut off from a man, it is considered dead (for ritual purity purposes), and when a man touches it, then for every part that contains a bone, the ritual bath (ghusl) becomes obligatory upon the one who touched it; and if there is no bone in it, then there is no ritual bath upon him.

key_terms.قِطْعَةٌ: A piece or part (of the body)
key_terms.مَيْتَةٌ: Dead (ritual status of the severed part)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on ghusl when touching a severed human body part?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the fiqh of *mayyitah* (corpse) regarding severed human parts, establishing that a limb is ritually impure as a whole body. It introduces a nuanced distinction in Shia jurisprudence where the obligation of *ghusl al-janabah* upon contact depends on the presence of bone, reflecting the scholarly view that bone signifies structural integrity akin to the living body. This ruling is particularly significant for understanding the purity status of remains in cases of violent death or partial burial.
